solution.description: Start by picking the nearest power of ten to 14. Here 10 is the closest, so every remaining step measures 14 against a base of 10.

solution.operation: Find the surplus from the base
solution.description: Measure the gap: 14 sits 4 above the base, so the surplus is +4. Keeping the sign matters, because it decides whether the left part grows or shrinks in step 4.

Set out the Yavadunam pattern for a square: the left part is the base plus twice the deviation, and the right part is the deviation multiplied by itself. Steps 4 and 5 fill in those two halves for 14, so no long multiplication is needed.
Double the surplus, 4 doubled is 8, and add it to the base: 10 plus 8 gives 18. That 18 is the left-hand block of the answer.
Now square the deviation itself: +4 times +4 is 16. Two like signs multiply to a positive, so the right-hand block is 16, and it has to fit the one-digit slot that base 10 provides.

solution.operation: Handle right part overflow (carry to left)
solution.result: \text{Right part } 16 \text{ has more than } 1 \text{ digit(s)} \\ \text{Carry } 1 \text{ to left: } 18 + 1 = 19 \\ \text{Keep } 6 \text{ as right part}
solution.description: 16 is wider than the one-digit slot, so it cannot all stay on the right. Keep the last one digits, 6, in the right block and carry the leading 1 into the left block, lifting 18 to 19.
Join the two blocks: write the left part 19 and follow it immediately with the one-digit right part 6. Read together they give 196, the square of 14.

solution.description: Start by picking the nearest power of ten to both factors. 96 and 97 both sit just under 100, so 100 is the shared base for the whole calculation.

solution.operation: Find the deficiencys from the base
solution.description: Measure each factor against the base: 96 is 4 below 100 and 97 is 3 below 100, giving deviations of -4 and -3. Both are negative because both factors are under the base.

solution.operation: Apply the Yavadunam Sutra formula for multiplication
solution.description: Set out the base-deviation pattern for a product: the left part is the base plus both deviations added in, and the right part is the two deviations multiplied together. Steps 4 and 5 fill in those two halves, replacing the usual long multiplication.

solution.operation: Compute the left part by cross-operation
solution.description: Cross-operate: add both deviations to the base, 100 plus -4 plus -3, which gives 93. The same 93 comes from either crosswise pairing, 96 minus 3 or 97 minus 4, which is a quick self-check on this block.

Multiply the two deviations together: -4 times -3 is 12. Both signs are negative, so the product is positive, and this 12 becomes the right-hand block sitting in the two-digit slot that base 100 provides.

solution.operation: Pad the right part to 2 digit(s)
solution.description: The base 100 ends in two zeros, so the right block must show exactly two digits. 12 already fills the slot exactly, so it needs no leading zero and there is nothing to carry into the left block.
Join the two blocks: write the left part 93 and follow it immediately with the two-digit right part 12. Read together they give 9312, the product of 96 and 97.
Check the shortcut against ordinary multiplication: working 96 times 97 out the long way also gives 9312, confirming that the cross-operation and the deviation product were both handled correctly.
